title: The names molluscs hide behind
standfirst: Molluscs goes by many names on a label. Here is the list we read for you.

spans.text: The law makes a maker name molluscs when they put it in on purpose. It does not make them use the word you are looking for.

blocks.label: names we watch for on a label
blocks.caption: Counted only where the link to molluscs is settled. Names that depend on the product are listed further down, and are not in this count.

resolved.method: Names whose link to mollusc is settled, counted from our allergen registry.
resolved.excludedNote: 11 more depend on the product or are shared with something else, so they are listed separately rather than counted here.

sources.doc: Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on the provision of food information to consumers, Annex II (list of substances or products causing allergies or intolerances), item 14: 'Molluscs and products thereof'
Food allergy and intolerance: the 14 allergens (molluscs listed as mussels, land snails, squid, whelks; oyster sauce named as a hidden source)

EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies (NDA): Scientific Opinion on the evaluation of allergenic foods and food ingredients for labelling purposes — molluscs (gastropods, bivalves, cephalopods) and tropomyosin as the major cross-reactive allergen

Food Allergen Labeling and Consumer Protection Act (FALCPA) — defines the U.S. major allergen 'Crustacean shellfish' ONLY; molluscan shellfish (clams, oysters, scallops, mussels) are NOT FALCPA major allergens, so U.S. labels may omit them
FASTER Act of 2021 — added sesame as the 9th U.S. major allergen; did not add molluscan shellfish (confirms the U.S. vs EU divergence)

Shellfish allergy overview — distinguishes crustacean shellfish from mollusks (bivalves: clams, mussels, oysters, scallops; gastropods: snails/abalone; cephalopods: squid/calamari, octopus, cuttlefish)

resolved.limit: We read what a label says. We cannot see what a maker left off it.

spans.text: These depend on the product. We treat them with care, and we say so on the label reading rather than guessing.
Names that look close but are not molluscs. These are the ones you can stop worrying about.
What we do when the label is unclear
If we cannot tell, we warn you. On this one thing we would rather be wrong in the direction of caution than quiet.
